docs.title: OTPHP
docs.text:
OTPHP computes and checks one-time passwords: the six digits an authenticator application shows your users for a second factor.

It implements both algorithms the specifications define. TOTP is time-based (RFC 6238) and is what almost every service uses. HOTP is counter-based (RFC 4226), the algorithm TOTP is built on. The codes are read by Google Authenticator, FreeOTP, Aegis, 1Password and the others.

use OTPHP\TOTP;

// Enrolment: one secret per account, stored with the account.
$totp = TOTP::generate($clock)
    ->withLabel('alice@example.com')
    ->withIssuer('My Service');

$user->setOtpSecret($totp->getSecret());
$uri = $totp->getProvisioningUri(); // the content of the QR code the user scans

use OTPHP\TOTP;

// Sign-in: the code the user typed, against the secret you stored.
$totp = TOTP::createFromSecret($user->getOtpSecret(), $clock);

if (! $totp->verify($code)) {
    throw new BadCredentialsException('Wrong code.');
}

docs.title: One package
docs.text:
composer require spomky-labs/otphp

It needs PHP 8.1 or later and nothing else of consequence: a Base32 codec, the psr/clock interface, and the deprecation contracts. No framework, no container, no database.

docs.title: What it does not do
docs.text: It does the arithmetic and nothing around it. Storing secrets, rendering QR codes, rate-limiting attempts and remembering which codes were already used are your application's work, and Security recommendations says what that work is. A library that only hands you the right digits cannot protect an account on its own.

docs.title: Where to start
docs.text:
• Installation to try it now.
  • TOTP or HOTP? if you are not sure which one you want. You almost certainly want TOTP.
  • What to store before you design your table. Storing the secret alone will cost you the day you change the number of digits.
  • Security recommendations before you ship.

docs.title: Authenticator applications
docs.text: The codes OTPHP produces are read by the applications users already have. What those applications will read is narrower than what the library can produce, and the difference is the most common cause of an enrolment that silently does not work.

docs.title: Google Authenticator
docs.text:
It supports exactly one configuration:

Parameter What it accepts Digest sha1 Digits 6 Period 30 seconds Epoch 0

Any other value is ignored, not refused. Hand it a URI with algorithm=sha512&digits=8&period=10 and it will scan happily, then show six SHA-1 digits every thirty seconds — codes your server will reject forever, with nothing anywhere to say why.

So if Google Authenticator is among the applications your users may install, keep the defaults:

use OTPHP\TOTP;

$totp = TOTP::generate($clock)        // sha1, 6 digits, 30 seconds
    ->withLabel('alice@example.com')
    ->withIssuer('My Service');

docs.title: The others
docs.text:
FreeOTP, Aegis, 2FAS, Ente Auth and the password managers generally read algorithm, digits and period. epoch and custom parameters are another matter: image is honoured by FreeOTP and ignored elsewhere, and no application reads a parameter of your own invention.

Nothing is guaranteed, and nothing announces what it supports. Before you move a live service off the defaults, test the applications your users actually have.

docs.title: Testing an enrolment by hand
docs.text:
The secret below is the one used throughout this documentation and in the RFC test vectors. It is public — never give it to a real account.

use OTPHP\TOTP;

$totp = TOTP::createFromSecret('JBSWY3DPEHPK3PXP', $clock)
    ->withLabel('alice@example.com')
    ->withIssuer('My Service');

echo $totp->getProvisioningUri();
echo $totp->now();
echo $totp->expiresIn();

Render that URI as a QR code on your own machine — see QR codes — scan it, and compare the digits on the phone with the ones now() printed. They match, or something in the list above explains why not.

If they differ by a constant that looks like a whole period, the device's clock is off. Most applications have a "time correction" or "sync" command for that; a reasonable window covers the rest.

docs.title: Say what you support
docs.text: Users choose their application before they read your documentation. One line next to the QR code — "works with Google Authenticator, FreeOTP, Aegis, 1Password and other TOTP applications" — prevents most of the support requests this page describes.

docs.title: QR codes
docs.text:
A user configures their application by scanning a QR code whose content is the provisioning URI. OTPHP does not draw that image: it hands you the string and leaves the rendering to a library of your choice.

Render it on your own server. The URI contains the secret, and sending it to a third party to be drawn hands over the second factor of that account.

docs.title: With BaconQrCode
docs.text:
BaconQrCode renders to PNG; its GDLibRenderer needs the gd extension.

composer require bacon/bacon-qr-code:^3.0

use BaconQrCode\Renderer\GDLibRenderer;
use BaconQrCode\Writer;
use OTPHP\TOTP;

$totp = TOTP::createFromSecret('JBSWY3DPEHPK3PXP', $clock)
    ->withLabel('alice@example.com')
    ->withIssuer('My Service');

$writer = new Writer(new GDLibRenderer(250));
$png = $writer->writeString($totp->getProvisioningUri());

echo '<img alt="" src="data:image/png;base64,' . base64_encode($png) . '">';

docs.title: With endroid/qr-code
docs.text:
endroid/qr-code has a builder and can return a data URI directly.

composer require endroid/qr-code

use Endroid\QrCode\Builder\Builder;
use Endroid\QrCode\Writer\PngWriter;
use OTPHP\TOTP;

$totp = TOTP::createFromSecret('JBSWY3DPEHPK3PXP', $clock)
    ->withLabel('alice@example.com')
    ->withIssuer('My Service');

$result = (new Builder(
    writer: new PngWriter(),
    data: $totp->getProvisioningUri(),
    size: 250,
))->build();

echo '<img alt="" src="' . $result->getDataUri() . '">';

A data URI keeps the image out of your routes and off your disk, which is one fewer place the secret can be fetched from later. If you do serve it from a URL instead, make that URL single-use and bound to the authenticated session.

docs.title: Show the secret as text too
docs.text: Some users cannot scan — a desktop password manager, a camera that will not focus, an application that imports keys by hand. Print the Base32 secret next to the image, in groups of four characters, and say which issuer and account it belongs to.

docs.title: Online generators
docs.text:
getQrCodeUri() builds the address of an external service, with the provisioning URI substituted into it. Both arguments are required: the template, and the placeholder to replace.

$url = $totp->getQrCodeUri(
    'https://api.qrserver.com/v1/create-qr-code/?data=[DATA]&size=300x300&ecc=M',
    '[DATA]'
);

echo '<img alt="" src="' . $url . '">';

This sends the secret to someone else

The URL-encoded provisioning URI travels to that service, in the query string of a request your user's browser makes. It may be logged by the service, cached by anything in between, and kept for as long as they please — and from it, anyone can generate valid codes for that account.

The method exists because it predates the alternatives. Use a local renderer. If a QR service is truly the only option available to you, satisfy yourself first that it neither caches nor logs what it is given, and understand that you are trusting it with a credential.

docs.title: Confirm before you enable
docs.text: Showing the QR code is not enrolment. Ask the user for one code produced by their application, verify it, and only then mark the factor as active. A code that fails here usually means a clock that is wrong on the device, which is worth saying in the error message.

docs.title: The factory
docs.text:
Factory does the opposite of getProvisioningUri(): it reads an otpauth:// URI and returns the object it describes, with every parameter already set.

use OTPHP\Factory;

$otp = Factory::loadFromProvisioningUri(
    'otpauth://totp/My%20Service%3Aalice%40example.com?issuer=My%20Service&secret=JBSWY3DPEHPK3PXP',
    $clock
);

$otp->verify($code);

It is the only public method of the class, and it is static.

docs.title: What you get back
docs.text:
A TOTP for otpauth://totp/…, a HOTP for otpauth://hotp/…. The declared return type is OTPInterface, so narrow it when you need the methods of one or the other:

use OTPHP\TOTPInterface;

$otp = Factory::loadFromProvisioningUri($uri, $clock);

if (! $otp instanceof TOTPInterface) {
    throw new LogicException('A time-based password was expected.');
}

echo $otp->expiresIn();

The clock is only used by a TOTP, and is optional today. It becomes mandatory in v12.0; omitting it emits a deprecation notice. See The clock.

docs.title: Everything comes back
docs.text:
The digest, the digits, the period, the epoch, the counter, the label, the issuer — and the custom parameters, unchanged:

$otp = Factory::loadFromProvisioningUri(
    'otpauth://totp/alice%40example.com?secret=JBSWY3DPEHPK3PXP&foo=bar',
    $clock
);

$otp->getParameter('foo');  // "bar"

Which is what makes storing the URI a complete record of an enrolment, rather than a secret plus a promise that nothing was configured differently. See What to store.

docs.title: The issuer, when the URI says it twice
docs.text:
The key URI format puts the issuer in two places — in front of the label, and as a query parameter — and some providers put different values in them. Microsoft Office 365 is the one you will meet.

Since v11.4, the query parameter wins:

$otp = Factory::loadFromProvisioningUri(
    'otpauth://totp/Microsoft%3Aalice%40example.com?secret=JBSWY3DPEHPK3PXP&issuer=Office365',
    $clock
);

$otp->getLabel();   // "alice@example.com"
$otp->getIssuer();  // "Office365"

Either way the prefix is stripped from the label, so getLabel() is the account name alone.

docs.title: What it refuses
docs.text:
InvalidProvisioningUriException — which extends InvalidArgumentException — for a URI that is not one:

  • a scheme other than otpauth;
  • a missing host, path or query string;
  • a type that is neither totp nor hotp;
  • no secret parameter.

A parameter that is present but invalid throws the exception of that parameter instead: InvalidParameterException for algorithm=md5 or digits=0, InvalidLabelException for a label that cannot be split. See Exceptions.

use OTPHP\Exception\OTPExceptionInterface;

try {
    $otp = Factory::loadFromProvisioningUri($uri, $clock);
} catch (OTPExceptionInterface $e) {
    // anything the library refuses, under one marker interface
}

Always wrap the call when the URI came from outside your own storage — a user pasting a URI, an import from another system. A valid-looking otpauth:// string is easy to produce and easy to get wrong.

docs.title: The provisioning URI
docs.text:
An authenticator application is configured by a single string: an otpauth:// URI holding the secret and every parameter needed to reproduce the codes. It is what a QR code carries.

use OTPHP\TOTP;

$totp = TOTP::createFromSecret('JBSWY3DPEHPK3PXP', $clock)
    ->withLabel('alice@example.com')
    ->withIssuer('My Service');

echo $totp->getProvisioningUri();

otpauth://totp/My%20Service%3Aalice%40example.com?issuer=My%20Service&secret=JBSWY3DPEHPK3PXP

Its shape is the key URI format Google Authenticator defined:

otpauth://<type>/<issuer>:<account>?<parameters>

The type is totp or hotp. The path is the label, with the issuer joined in front of it by a colon when there is one. The parameters carry the rest, sorted by name.

docs.title: A label is required
docs.text: getProvisioningUri() throws InvalidLabelException when neither a label nor an issuer is set: there would be nothing to name the account with. Set the label before you call it. See The label and the issuer.

docs.title: Defaults are left out
docs.text:
A parameter at its default value is omitted, because an application that does not read it will assume the same default anyway:

$totp->withPeriod(30)->getProvisioningUri();  // no "period="
$totp->withPeriod(60)->getProvisioningUri();  // "period=60"
$totp->withEpoch(0)->getProvisioningUri();    // no "epoch="

A fully specified TOTP looks like this:

otpauth://totp/My%20Service%3Aalice%40example.com?algorithm=sha512&digits=8&issuer=My%20Service&period=10&secret=JBSWY3DPEHPK3PXP

And a HOTP carries its counter, which is never omitted:

otpauth://hotp/alice%40example.com?counter=1000&secret=JBSWY3DPEHPK3PXP

docs.title: It is the secret, written out
docs.text: Treat the URI exactly as you treat the secret. It goes to the user's browser once, over TLS, in a page that is not cached; it does not go into a log, an exception message, an analytics event or a third-party service. QR codes is about the last of those.

docs.title: It round-trips
docs.text:
Everything the URI holds — the custom parameters included — can be read back into an equivalent object:

use OTPHP\Factory;

$otp = Factory::loadFromProvisioningUri($uri, $clock);

Which makes the URI a reasonable thing to store, instead of the secret and a scattering of columns. See The factory and What to store.

docs.title: Exceptions
docs.text:
Every exception the library throws implements OTPHP\Exception\OTPExceptionInterface, and every one of them also extends a standard PHP exception. So you can catch the library as a whole, catch one precise failure, or keep the catch (InvalidArgumentException) you already had — all three work.

use OTPHP\Exception\OTPExceptionInterface;

try {
    $otp = Factory::loadFromProvisioningUri($uri, $clock);
} catch (OTPExceptionInterface $e) {
    // anything this library refuses
}
Exception Extends Thrown when InvalidParameterException InvalidArgumentException A parameter has an invalid value InvalidLabelException InvalidArgumentException A label or issuer breaks the key URI grammar InvalidProvisioningUriException InvalidArgumentException An otpauth:// URI cannot be read ParameterNotFoundException InvalidArgumentException A parameter that was never set is read SecretDecodingException RuntimeException A secret is not valid Base32

A wrong code is not an exception. verify() returns false.

docs.title: InvalidParameterException
docs.text:
The one you will meet most. It carries the name and the value that were refused, as public readonly properties:

use OTPHP\Exception\InvalidParameterException;

try {
    $totp = $totp->withDigits($request->get('digits'));
} catch (InvalidParameterException $e) {
    $e->getMessage();      // "Digits must be between 1 and 10."
    $e->parameterName;     // "digits"
    $e->parameterValue;    // 0
}

It covers secret, algorithm, digits, period, epoch, counter, secretSize, timestamp, leeway and the internal timecode. The rules each of them enforces are on the pages of The parameters.

docs.title: InvalidLabelException
docs.text:
Same shape, with labelName and labelValue:

use OTPHP\Exception\InvalidLabelException;

try {
    $totp = $totp->withLabel('user:invalid:format');
} catch (InvalidLabelException $e) {
    $e->getMessage();   // "Neither issuer nor account name in label may contain a colon."
    $e->labelName;      // "label"
    $e->labelValue;     // "user:invalid:format"
}

It is also what getProvisioningUri() throws when no label and no issuer are set, and when the label contains a colon. See The label and the issuer.

docs.title: InvalidProvisioningUriException
docs.text:
From the factory: a scheme that is not otpauth, a missing host, path or query, a type other than totp or hotp, or no secret.

use OTPHP\Exception\InvalidProvisioningUriException;

try {
    $otp = Factory::loadFromProvisioningUri('invalid-uri', $clock);
} catch (InvalidProvisioningUriException $e) {
    $e->getMessage();   // "Not a valid OTP provisioning URI"
}

A URI whose shape is right but whose values are not throws the exception of the offending parameter instead — algorithm=md5 throws InvalidParameterException. Catch OTPExceptionInterface if you only want to know that the URI was unusable.

docs.title: ParameterNotFoundException
docs.text:
getParameter() throws rather than returning null, so a typo cannot pass for an absent value:

use OTPHP\Exception\ParameterNotFoundException;

try {
    $totp->getParameter('nonexistent');
} catch (ParameterNotFoundException $e) {
    $e->parameterName;  // "nonexistent"
}

hasParameter() asks the same question without the exception.

docs.title: SecretDecodingException
docs.text:
A RuntimeException, not an InvalidArgumentException, because of when it happens: the secret is decoded the first time a code is computed, not when it is set. An invalid secret is accepted by createFromSecret() and fails at now(), at() or verify().

use OTPHP\Exception\SecretDecodingException;

$totp = TOTP::createFromSecret('INVALID!@#', $clock);   // no exception here

try {
    $totp->now();                                       // here
} catch (SecretDecodingException $e) {
    // "Unable to decode the secret. Is it correctly base32 encoded?"
}

To validate a secret a user typed, generate a code from it. Constructing the object proves nothing.

docs.title: Catching precisely
docs.text:
use OTPHP\Exception\InvalidParameterException;
use OTPHP\Exception\InvalidProvisioningUriException;

try {
    $otp = Factory::loadFromProvisioningUri($uri, $clock);
    $valid = $otp->verify($code);
} catch (InvalidProvisioningUriException $e) {
    $logger->error('Stored provisioning URI is unusable.', ['user' => $user->getId()]);
} catch (InvalidParameterException $e) {
    $logger->error('Refused parameter.', ['name' => $e->parameterName]);
}

Two habits worth keeping. Do not put the message in an HTTP response: these messages exist to be read by you, and $e->parameterValue may hold the secret. Do not log the URI or the secret — see Security recommendations.

docs.title: Nothing to migrate
docs.text: These classes arrived without breaking anything. Each extends the standard exception that was thrown before, the messages are unchanged, and existing catch (InvalidArgumentException) and catch (RuntimeException) blocks keep working. Move to the specific types when it helps you, at your own pace.

docs.title: My codes do not last the full period
docs.text:
They never do, and they are not meant to. A TOTP is valid for its period, not for the period that begins when you ask for it. The boundaries are fixed by the clock:

timecode = floor((timestamp - epoch) / period)

With the default thirty seconds, the code changes at every multiple of thirty of Unix time. Ask for one at second 29 and it has one second left. This loop prints two different codes:

use OTPHP\TOTP;

$totp = TOTP::createFromSecret($secret, $clock)->withPeriod(10);

for ($i = 0; $i < 10; $i++) {
    echo $totp->now(), "\n";
    sleep(1);
}

expiresIn() says how many seconds remain. Show it next to the code, and allow a small window for the user who typed one that had just turned over.

docs.title: A user's codes are always refused, although their application scanned the QR code
docs.text:
Three usual causes, in order of likelihood:

  1. The device's clock is wrong. Most applications offer a time correction or sync command. A window of a few seconds absorbs the rest.
  2. Your parameters are not the ones their application reads. Google Authenticator ignores algorithm, digits, period and epoch, and silently shows six SHA-1 digits every thirty seconds. See Authenticator applications.
  3. You rebuilt the object with the wrong parameters. createFromSecret() returns the defaults; if the account was provisioned with eight digits you must set eight again. This is what storing the provisioning URI prevents.

docs.title: Can a code be used twice?
docs.text:
A TOTP, yes — and that is your problem to solve, not the library's. It has no memory: a code it accepted at the start of a period it accepts again until the period ends, and for the whole window on top. Store the last accepted timecode with the account and refuse anything that is not newer.

A HOTP, no, provided you persist the counter. verify() advances it past the code that matched, so that code and every earlier one are dead. See The counter.

docs.title: Is there a Symfony bundle?
docs.text: No, and none is needed. The library has no service to configure: build a TOTP where you need one and inject a PSR-20 clock, which symfony/clock provides. Two or three lines in your own service is the whole integration.

docs.title: How do I test code that verifies a TOTP?
docs.text:
Inject a clock you control. With a fixed clock the code becomes a constant you can assert:

use OTPHP\TOTP;
use Symfony\Component\Clock\MockClock;

$clock = new MockClock(new DateTimeImmutable('@1519401289'));
$totp = TOTP::createFromSecret('JBSWY3DPEHPK3PXP', $clock);

self::assertSame('626112', $totp->now());

See The clock.

docs.title: Why is the generated secret 103 characters long?
docs.text:
The default is 64 random bytes, and Base32 turns them into 103 characters. It is more than anything needs: the strength is capped by the digest anyway, and a long secret makes a denser QR code that some cameras read badly. Pass a size — 20 bytes is what RFC 4226 recommends:

$totp = TOTP::generate($clock, 20);  // 32 characters

See The secret.

docs.title: Can I use OTPHP for a code sent by e-mail or text message?
docs.text:
You can, with care. Set the epoch to the moment you generate the code and the period to how long it should live, and the code is valid for exactly that span.

Use a fresh secret for every code. With a fixed secret and the epoch set to the creation time, the timecode is always 0 and you would send the same digits every time.

A single-use token in a table is simpler and does the same job. Reach for this only if you have a reason.

docs.title: Why was my digest refused?
docs.text: Because it produces fewer than 19 bytes, or because it is not an HMAC algorithm. The RFC 4226 truncation reads up to the 19th byte of the digest, so a shorter hash — md5, ripemd128 — would be read past its end and collapse the code onto a handful of values. Since v11.5 the library refuses rather than compute that. Use sha1, sha256 or sha512. See The digest and the digits.

docs.title: Why do I get a deprecation notice about $clock?
docs.text: Because a TOTP was built without one. It becomes mandatory in v12.0; pass a PSR-20 clock to generate(), createFromSecret(), the constructor and Factory::loadFromProvisioningUri(). See The clock.

docs.title: Why do I get a deprecation notice about setDigits()?
docs.text: Because the mutable setters are deprecated since v11.4 and removed in v12.0, when the classes become readonly. Replace $otp->setX(…) with $otp = $otp->withX(…) — and do not forget the assignment. See From v11 to v12.

docs.title: Can the same object be a TOTP and a HOTP?
docs.text: No. They are separate classes with separate algorithms, and a provisioning URI names one of the two. Nothing stops an application from using both for different purposes.

docs.title: What to store
docs.text: To check a code you must rebuild the same object the user's application holds. Which means your database has to remember not only the secret, but every parameter that went into it. There are two ways to do that, and the easy one has a cost you pay later.

docs.title: The columns approach
docs.text:
Store the secret, and keep the parameters in your code:

use OTPHP\TOTP;

$totp = TOTP::createFromSecret($user->getOtpSecret(), $clock)
    ->withDigest('sha1')
    ->withDigits(6)
    ->withPeriod(30);

$totp->verify($code);

This works, for exactly as long as those three values never change. The day you decide that six digits should become eight, or that sha1 should become sha256, or that thirty seconds should become twenty, every existing account stops authenticating — their applications keep producing codes for the old configuration, and your server now computes the new one. Custom parameters set at enrolment are lost the same way.

If you take this route, store the parameters as columns rather than constants, and read them back per account. That is the whole of the problem: the parameters belong to the enrolment, not to the current version of your code.

docs.title: The provisioning URI approach
docs.text:
Store the provisioning URI itself. It holds the secret and every parameter, custom ones included, in one text column:

use OTPHP\Factory;

$otp = Factory::loadFromProvisioningUri($user->getProvisioningUri(), $clock);

$otp->verify($code);

A change of policy now affects only the accounts enrolled after it. Old URIs keep working, and you can re-provision them at your own pace — the next time each user signs in, for instance.

This is the approach to take.

For HOTP, write it back

A successful verify() advances the counter, and the URI you stored still carries the old one. Save the new URI after every successful verification, or the counter never moves and the replay protection is not there:

if ($otp->verify($code, null, 5)) {
    $user->setProvisioningUri($otp->getProvisioningUri());
    $entityManager->flush();
}

A TOTP has no such state and needs no write.

docs.title: Either way
docs.text:
Encrypt the column. Secret or URI, it is a credential that yields valid codes to anyone who reads it, and unlike a password hash it cannot be made useless by a one-way function. Encrypt at rest, with a key that does not live in the same database.

Keep a little state of your own, which no column above gives you:

What Why The last accepted timecode, or code So a TOTP cannot be replayed within its period A failure counter, per account So six digits are not brute-forced at leisure Whether enrolment was confirmed So a QR code nobody scanned does not lock the account When the factor was added For the security page, and for support

Security recommendations covers each of these.

docs.title: From v10 to v11
docs.text:
Nothing to change in your code. The release requires PHP 8.1 or later, and no API changed.

One behaviour did, and it is one you may be passing a value to.

docs.title: The TOTP window is no longer counted in periods
docs.text:
In v10, the window was a number of periods, applied on both sides. The range went from timestamp - window × period to timestamp + window × period: with a window of 5 and a period of 30, every code in the five periods before and the five after was accepted — eleven codes in all.

In v11, the window is a number of seconds, and three timestamps are tested: timestamp - window, timestamp, timestamp + window. It models clock drift rather than a range of periods. The window must be strictly smaller than the period; a larger one throws InvalidParameterException.

// v10: with a 30-second period, this accepted 11 codes
$totp->verify($code, null, 5);

// v11: this accepts the code of the current period, and of the previous
// or the next one if 20 seconds of drift reach into it
$totp->verify($code, null, 20);

So a window value carried over from v10 means something quite different now: with a thirty-second period, a window of 5 went from accepting eleven codes to accepting the current one — and a neighbouring one only in the five seconds either side of a boundary. A value that was legal there may also be refused now, since any window equal to or greater than the period throws. Re-read every call that passes a third argument. See The window.

The HOTP window is unchanged: it is still a number of counters, scanned upwards from the current one.

docs.title: From v11 to v12
docs.text:
Three changes. One has already landed, in v11.5; the other two are deprecations in v11.4 that become breaking in v12.0. All three can be dealt with today, on v11, which is the point of this page.

Change Lands in Impact Digests shorter than 19 bytes are refused v11.5 Only configurations using one, such as md5 The set*() methods go, classes become readonly v12.0 High, if you use setters The PSR-20 clock becomes mandatory for TOTP v12.0 High, for every TOTP

Upgrading to the latest v11 with no deprecation notices left means v12.0 will be a version bump and nothing more.

docs.title: Short digests are refused, since v11.5
docs.text:
This one is already in effect, and it is a security fix, not a deprecation. A digest shorter than 19 bytes is rejected by both entry points:

// Direct configuration
TOTP::generate($clock)->withDigest('md5');
// InvalidParameterException

// A provisioning URI
Factory::loadFromProvisioningUri(
    'otpauth://totp/Foo%3Aalice%40example.com?algorithm=md5&secret=JDDK4U6G3BJLEZ7Y',
    $clock
);
// InvalidProvisioningUriException

Why. The RFC 4226 truncation reads four bytes at an offset between 0 and 15 — up to the 19th byte of the digest. With a 16-byte hash it reads past the end, and the code collapses onto a small set of values that barely depend on the secret. That is a real weakness in the verification path. Such algorithms are also outside RFC 4226 and RFC 6238, and no authenticator application reads them.

The validation now uses hash_hmac_algos() rather than hash_algos(), which additionally rejects non-HMAC algorithms such as crc32 and adler32. Those used to pass validation and then fail inside hash_hmac().

What to do. Move to a supported digest:

// Before
$totp = $totp->withDigest('md5');

// After
$totp = $totp->withDigest('sha256');

Accounts provisioned with md5 were never safe and never interoperable. They must be re-enrolled; their secrets cannot simply be re-labelled with a new algorithm, because the codes would change. See The digest and the digits.

docs.title: The setters go, and the classes become readonly
docs.text:
Every set*() method is deprecated since v11.4 and removed in v12.0. Each has an immutable twin that returns a new object instead of mutating the one you hold.

Deprecated Replacement setSecret(string): void withSecret(string): self setDigits(int): void withDigits(int): self setDigest(string): void withDigest(string): self setLabel(string): void withLabel(string): self setIssuer(string): void withIssuer(string): self setIssuerIncludedAsParameter(bool): void withIssuerIncludedAsParameter(bool): self setParameter(string, mixed): void withParameter(string, mixed): self setPeriod(int): void (TOTP) withPeriod(int): self setEpoch(int): void (TOTP) withEpoch(int): self setCounter(int): void (HOTP) withCounter(int): self 
use OTPHP\TOTP;

// v11.3 and earlier
$totp = TOTP::generate($clock);
$totp->setLabel('alice@example.com');
$totp->setIssuer('My Service');
$totp->setDigits(8);

// v11.4 and later
$totp = TOTP::generate($clock)
    ->withLabel('alice@example.com')
    ->withIssuer('My Service')
    ->withDigits(8);

Reassign the result

A with*() call whose result is thrown away does nothing you can see. This is the one mistake the change introduces, and no deprecation notice will catch it:

$otp->withDigits(8);         // lost
$otp = $otp->withDigits(8);  // kept

docs.title: Patterns
docs.text:
// Several parameters
$otp = $otp->withSecret('NEWSECRET')->withDigits(8);

// Conditionally
if ($useCustomLabel) {
    $otp = $otp->withLabel($customLabel);
}

// Advancing a HOTP counter
$hotp = $hotp->withCounter($hotp->getCounter() + 1);

docs.title: Finding them
docs.text:
grep -rn -- '->set[A-Z]' --include='*.php' src/ | grep -v vendor

A test that the migration worked, rather than one that only exercises the new names:

$original = TOTP::generate($clock);
$modified = $original->withLabel('alice@example.com');

self::assertNotSame($original, $modified);
self::assertNull($original->getLabel());
self::assertSame('alice@example.com', $modified->getLabel());

docs.title: One exception: HOTP keeps mutating
docs.text: HOTP::verify() advances the counter on success, and will keep doing so. HOTP is the one class not marked @readonly, because that mutation is what prevents a code from being accepted twice. It is not something to migrate away from — but you do have to persist the new counter. See The counter.

docs.title: The clock becomes mandatory
docs.text:
A TOTP reads the time from a PSR-20 ClockInterface. Passing null works today, emits a deprecation notice, and falls back to the library's internal clock. In v12.0 the argument is required.

Four places take it:

new TOTP($secret, $clock);
TOTP::generate($clock, $secretSize);
TOTP::createFromSecret($secret, $clock);
Factory::loadFromProvisioningUri($uri, $clock);

use OTPHP\TOTP;
use Symfony\Component\Clock\NativeClock;

// Deprecated
$totp = TOTP::generate();

// What to write
$totp = TOTP::generate(new NativeClock());

The notice to watch for in your logs:

The parameter "$clock" will become mandatory in 12.0.0.
Please set a valid PSR Clock implementation instead of "null".

docs.title: Which implementation
docs.text:
Any PSR-20 one, from your application rather than from the library:

composer require symfony/clock

use Symfony\Component\Clock\NativeClock;
use Symfony\Component\Clock\MockClock;

$clock = new NativeClock();                                     // production
$clock = new MockClock(new DateTimeImmutable('@1519401289'));   // tests

lcobucci/clock works just as well. OTPHP\InternalClock is marked @internal and sits outside the backwards compatibility policy — it is the fallback the library uses for you, not a class to depend on. See The clock.

docs.title: Finding the calls
docs.text:
grep -rn 'TOTP::generate()\|TOTP::create(\|new TOTP(\|loadFromProvisioningUri(' --include='*.php' src/

Then run your test suite and read the deprecation notices. None left means nothing left to do.

HOTP is unaffected: it counts uses, not seconds.

docs.title: The timeline
docs.text: Version What happened v11.1 create() deprecated, in favour of generate() and createFromSecret() v11.3 The clock argument introduced, optional v11.4 with*() added, set*() deprecated; a deprecation notice when no clock is passed v11.5 Digests shorter than 19 bytes, and non-HMAC algorithms, refused v12.0 Classes readonly, set*() removed, the clock mandatory

docs.title: If something is stuck
docs.text: Search the existing issues, then open a new one with the version you are on, the code that breaks and the message you get. A security issue goes to security@spomky-labs.com instead.

docs.title: From v8.3 to v9
docs.text:
Only the way objects are built changed.

Along with it: every class became final, the minimum PHP version became 7.1, strict type hints were added throughout, and HHVM stopped being tested.

docs.title: Constructors became private
docs.text:
Build objects through the static methods.

use OTPHP\TOTP;

// Before
$otp = new TOTP();

// After
$otp = TOTP::create();

create() has itself been deprecated since v11.1, in favour of generate() and createFromSecret(). If you are coming from v8.3 today, go straight to those — see Creating an OTP.

docs.title: The label left the constructor
docs.text:
It was the first argument; it has a method of its own.

use OTPHP\TOTP;

// Before
$otp = new TOTP($label);

// After
$otp = TOTP::create();
$otp->setLabel($label);

The other parameters are unchanged.

setLabel() is in turn deprecated since v11.4; withLabel() replaces it. See The label and the issuer.

docs.title: From v9 to v10
docs.text:
Normally nothing to do. The release updated the dependencies and raised the minimum PHP version to 7.2.

What changed:

  • New public methods on the interfaces.
  • A dedicated interface for the factory, FactoryInterface.
  • Both arguments of getQrCodeUri() became required. The Google Charts API it used to default to was deprecated in April 2019, so there is no sensible default left to fall back on. Pass the URI of the service and the placeholder to replace in it — or, better, render the QR code yourself. See QR codes.
  • The mbstring extension became a required dependency. It no longer is: v11 calls nothing from it.

docs.title: Creating an OTP
docs.text: There are two moments in the life of an account where you build an OTP object, and they call different methods: enrolment, where the secret does not exist yet, and verification, where it does.

docs.title: At enrolment: a new secret
docs.text:
generate() draws a secret from random_bytes() and returns an object around it.

use OTPHP\TOTP;
use OTPHP\HOTP;

$totp = TOTP::generate($clock);     // 64 random bytes, Base32-encoded
$hotp = HOTP::generate();           // HOTP needs no clock

$secret = $totp->getSecret();       // what you store with the account

A second argument sets the size of the secret, in bytes:

$totp = TOTP::generate($clock, 20); // 20 bytes, 32 Base32 characters

See The secret for what size to pick and why the default is large.

docs.title: At verification: an existing secret
docs.text:
createFromSecret() takes the Base32 secret you stored.

use OTPHP\TOTP;

$totp = TOTP::createFromSecret($user->getOtpSecret(), $clock);

The object comes with the default parameters — sha1, six digits, a thirty-second period — so if you provisioned the account with anything else, you must set it back:

$totp = TOTP::createFromSecret($user->getOtpSecret(), $clock)
    ->withDigest('sha256')
    ->withDigits(8);

Carrying those three lines around is how parameters drift apart. The alternative is to store the whole provisioning URI and let the factory rebuild the object from it. What to store compares the two.

docs.title: Setting the parameters
docs.text:
Every parameter has a with*() method that returns a new object, so they chain:

use OTPHP\TOTP;

$totp = TOTP::generate($clock)
    ->withLabel('alice@example.com')
    ->withIssuer('My Service')
    ->withDigest('sha256')
    ->withDigits(8)
    ->withPeriod(30);

The matching set*() methods mutate the object in place. They are deprecated since v11.4 and removed in v12.0, when the classes become readonly. Write with*() in new code; see From v11 to v12.

docs.title: The deprecated constructors
docs.text:
TOTP::create() and HOTP::create() take every parameter positionally and have been deprecated since v11.1:

// Deprecated since v11.1
$totp = TOTP::create('JBSWY3DPEHPK3PXP', 30, 'sha1', 6);

// What to write instead
$totp = TOTP::createFromSecret('JBSWY3DPEHPK3PXP', $clock)
    ->withPeriod(30)
    ->withDigest('sha1')
    ->withDigits(6);

The constructors themselves are not public API: new TOTP(...) works but says nothing about which parameters the object ends up with. Use the static methods.

docs.title: Generating a password
docs.text: Your server normally generates codes only to compare them with what a user typed, which verify() does for you. The methods below are for the cases where you need the code itself: a test, a diagnostic page, or an OTP you send yourself through another channel.

docs.title: The current code
docs.text:
now(), on a TOTP, reads the clock and returns the code of the current period.

use OTPHP\TOTP;

$totp = TOTP::createFromSecret('JBSWY3DPEHPK3PXP', $clock);

echo $totp->now();       // the six digits of the current period

docs.title: How long it lasts
docs.text:
expiresIn() returns the number of seconds before the code changes.

echo $totp->expiresIn(); // 17, say

It is the remainder of the period, not a countdown from when you asked. A code read one second before the boundary lives for one second, which is why an interface that shows the code should show this number next to it — and why a user who types the code of the previous period is not being careless. See The window.

docs.title: A code at a given input
docs.text:
at() takes the input directly: a Unix timestamp for a TOTP, a counter value for a HOTP.

use OTPHP\TOTP;
use OTPHP\HOTP;

$totp = TOTP::createFromSecret('JBSWY3DPEHPK3PXP', $clock);
echo $totp->at(1_519_401_289);  // "626112": the code of the period holding that second

$hotp = HOTP::createFromSecret('JBSWY3DPEHPK3PXP');
echo $hotp->at(0);              // "282760", the first code
echo $hotp->at(1);              // "996554", the second

at() does not move anything. Calling it on a HOTP leaves the counter where it was; only verify() advances it.

Both reject a negative input, and a TOTP also rejects a timestamp earlier than its epoch: there is no period before the beginning. Both throw InvalidParameterException.

docs.title: How the digits are computed
docs.text:
For the record, since it explains two constraints you will meet elsewhere. The library follows RFC 4226 §5.3: it computes HMAC(secret, input), reads the low four bits of the last byte of the digest as an offset, takes the four bytes at that offset, masks the top bit off, and keeps the last n decimal digits of the 31-bit number that remains.

That offset can be as high as 15, so the truncation reads up to the 19th byte — which is why a digest shorter than 19 bytes is refused. And 31 bits hold at most ten digits, which is why ten is the maximum. See The digest and the digits.

docs.title: The clock
docs.text:
A time-based password is a function of the current time, so a TOTP needs to know what the current time is. It does not call time(): it reads a PSR-20 ClockInterface you give it.

use OTPHP\TOTP;
use Symfony\Component\Clock\NativeClock;

$totp = TOTP::generate(new NativeClock());

A HOTP counts uses rather than seconds and takes no clock at all.

docs.title: Pass it everywhere a TOTP is built
docs.text:
Four entry points accept it, and all four are optional today:

new TOTP($secret, $clock);
TOTP::generate($clock, $secretSize);
TOTP::createFromSecret($secret, $clock);
Factory::loadFromProvisioningUri($uri, $clock);

Omitting it triggers a deprecation notice and falls back to the library's own clock. In v12.0 it becomes mandatory, and omitting it will be a TypeError. Pass it now; the deprecation notice reads:

The parameter "$clock" will become mandatory in 12.0.0.
Please set a valid PSR Clock implementation instead of "null".

Finding the places that still omit it:

grep -rn 'TOTP::generate()\|TOTP::createFromSecret(\|new TOTP(\|loadFromProvisioningUri(' --include='*.php' src/

docs.title: Which implementation
docs.text:
Any PSR-20 one. symfony/clock and lcobucci/clock both provide one, and a project that already has either needs nothing more:

composer require symfony/clock

use Symfony\Component\Clock\NativeClock;

$clock = new NativeClock();

Inject it into your own services instead of constructing it where you need it. That one habit is what makes the next section possible.

OTPHP\InternalClock is not for your code

The library ships a minimal ClockInterface and uses it as the fallback when you pass null. It is marked @internal, which puts it outside the backwards compatibility policy: it may change or disappear in a minor release. Depend on a clock from your application, not on that class.

docs.title: Deciding what time it is, in a test
docs.text:
This is the reason the clock is an argument. With a fixed clock, a TOTP becomes a pure function and its code becomes an assertable value:

use OTPHP\TOTP;
use Symfony\Component\Clock\MockClock;

// 1519401289 is 2018-02-23 15:54:49 UTC. A timestamp leaves no room for a timezone to surprise you.
$clock = new MockClock(new DateTimeImmutable('@1519401289'));
$totp = TOTP::createFromSecret('JBSWY3DPEHPK3PXP', $clock);

self::assertSame('626112', $totp->now());

$clock->sleep(30);
self::assertSame('567611', $totp->now());

The same trick tests the parts that are otherwise awkward: a code at the very end of its period, a device whose clock drifts by twenty seconds, a window that is too wide.

The epoch is the other half of this. It shifts where periods begin, and is covered in The period and the epoch.

docs.title: The window
docs.text:
The third argument of verify() widens what counts as valid. It exists for two real problems — a phone whose clock is a few seconds off, and a hardware token whose button was pressed in a pocket — and for nothing else. Each unit of window is another code an attacker gets to guess with, so keep it small.

By default it is null: one code is tested, and that is all.

docs.title: TOTP: seconds of drift
docs.text:
For a TOTP the window is a number of seconds, not of periods. Three timestamps are tested, in this order:

timestamp - window
timestamp
timestamp + window

So a window accepts the previous code when timestamp - window falls into the previous period, and the next one when timestamp + window falls into the next. It does not accept everything in between — the range is sampled at three points, not scanned.

// At second 1476822005, with a 30-second period, the current period runs from 1476822000
// to 1476822029. The previous code was the one of 1476821970 to 1476821999.

$totp->verify($previousCode);            // false: only 1476822005 is tested
$totp->verify($previousCode, null, 5);   // false: 1476822000 is still in the current period
$totp->verify($previousCode, null, 20);  // true: 1476821985 is in the previous one

The window must be smaller than the period. A window equal to or larger than it would reach past the adjacent periods and is rejected with InvalidParameterException:

$totp = TOTP::createFromSecret($secret, $clock)->withPeriod(30);

$totp->verify($code, null, 30); // InvalidParameterException

A window that would make timestamp - window negative is rejected too.

How much to allow: enough to cover a device whose clock was never synchronised, which in practice is a few seconds to half a period. The sign of the window does not matter — it is taken as an absolute value.

docs.title: HOTP: counters ahead
docs.text:
For a HOTP the window is a number of counters, and they are scanned one by one from the current counter upwards:

counter, counter + 1, …, counter + window

$hotp = HOTP::createFromSecret($secret)->withCounter(1000);

$hotp->verify($codeFor1003);          // false: only 1000 is tested
$hotp->verify($codeFor1003, null, 5); // true: 1000 to 1005 are tested

The first match wins, and the counter moves to just past it: after the second call above, getCounter() returns 1004. The codes that were skipped are gone for good, which is the point — it is how the server catches up with a device that produced codes nobody submitted.

A window of five to ten covers accidental presses. A very large one turns a single stolen code into a valid one for a long stretch of the counter space.

docs.title: A note for readers coming from v10
docs.text: In version 10 the TOTP window was a number of periods, applied on both sides: a window of 5 with a 30-second period accepted the five codes before and the five after. Version 11 changed it to the seconds of drift described above. If you carried a window value across that upgrade, re-read it — see From v10 to v11.

docs.title: TOTP or HOTP?
docs.text:
Both algorithms hash a secret together with a counter and truncate the result to a few digits. They differ only in where the counter comes from.

TOTP HOTP The counter is the clock, divided into periods a number you keep, incremented at each use A code is valid for the length of the period until it is used Both sides must agree on the time how many codes have been consumed Goes out of sync when a clock drifts a code is generated but not submitted Used by nearly every service with a second factor hardware tokens, and little else

You want TOTP. It is what Google Authenticator, FreeOTP, Aegis, 1Password and the rest show by default, and what a user expects when you say "authenticator app". Choose HOTP only when something outside your application already requires it.

docs.title: TOTP
docs.text:
The current timecode is the number of whole periods elapsed since the epoch, by default the Unix epoch:

timecode = floor((timestamp - epoch) / period)

The code changes when that number does. With the default thirty-second period, it changes at every multiple of thirty seconds of Unix time — which is why a code shown to the user may have one second of life left. expiresIn() says how many seconds remain.

Synchronisation is a matter of clocks. The server's clock is yours to keep right; the device's clock is not, and the window is what absorbs a small difference.

use OTPHP\TOTP;

$totp = TOTP::generate($clock);
echo $totp->now();

docs.title: HOTP
docs.text:
The counter starts at zero and advances by one each time a code is accepted. verify() performs that advance itself, and that is deliberate: it is what stops a code from being used twice.

use OTPHP\HOTP;

$hotp = HOTP::generate();

if ($hotp->verify($code)) {
    $user->setOtpCounter($hotp->getCounter()); // persist it, or you lose the protection
}

The two sides fall out of step whenever the device produces a code that never reaches the server — a button pressed in a pocket. The window lets the server catch up by looking a few counters ahead.

Nothing prevents using both, for different purposes, in the same application. They share a parent class and almost all of their API.

docs.title: Verifying a password
docs.text:
verify() answers one question: does this code match this secret, at this moment. It returns a boolean and never throws for a wrong code.

use OTPHP\TOTP;

$totp = TOTP::createFromSecret($user->getOtpSecret(), $clock);

if (! $totp->verify($code)) {
    // wrong code
}

The comparison itself uses hash_equals(), so a wrong code takes the same time to reject whatever digit it got wrong.

docs.title: Its three arguments
docs.text:
The signature is the same for both algorithms, and the second argument is what differs:

public function verify(string $otp, null|int $input = null, null|int $window = null): bool;
TOTP HOTP $input A Unix timestamp. Defaults to the clock's A counter. Defaults to the object's $window Seconds of accepted clock drift How many counters ahead to look

Leave both at null and you get the strictest check: the code of the current period, or of the current counter, and nothing else.

docs.title: TOTP
docs.text:
$totp->verify($code);                   // at the current second
$totp->verify($code, 1_519_401_289);    // at that second instead
$totp->verify($code, null, 10);         // allowing ten seconds of drift

A TOTP has no state, so verifying it changes nothing. The same code passes again for the rest of its period, and for the whole window on top of it — your application is what must refuse it a second time. See Security recommendations.

It throws InvalidParameterException when the timestamp is negative, when the window is not smaller than the period, or when the window would push the timestamp below zero.

docs.title: HOTP
docs.text:
$hotp = HOTP::createFromSecret($user->getOtpSecret())
    ->withCounter($user->getOtpCounter());

if ($hotp->verify($code, null, 5)) {
    $user->setOtpCounter($hotp->getCounter()); // required
    $entityManager->flush();
}

A HOTP is stateful. On success, verify() sets the counter to one past the value that matched, so the accepted code — and every code before it — can never be accepted again. HOTP is the one class in the library that is not @readonly, for exactly this reason.

That protection only survives if you write the new counter back. Read it with getCounter() after a successful verification and persist it; a request that forgets to will accept the same code again.

Passing a counter lower than the object's returns false without testing anything: counters move forward only.

docs.title: Which codes are accepted
docs.text: Exactly one, unless you pass a window — and then a few more, in a way worth knowing precisely. See The window.

docs.title: Custom parameters
docs.text:
Any name that is not one of the library's own can be set on an OTP object. It is kept, it appears in the provisioning URI, and it comes back when the factory reads that URI.

use OTPHP\TOTP;

$totp = TOTP::createFromSecret('JBSWY3DPEHPK3PXP', $clock)
    ->withLabel('alice@example.com')
    ->withParameter('foo', 'bar');

echo $totp->getProvisioningUri();

otpauth://totp/alice%40example.com?foo=bar&secret=JBSWY3DPEHPK3PXP

Reading it:

$totp->hasParameter('foo');   // true
$totp->getParameter('foo');   // "bar"
$totp->getParameters();        // every parameter, the library's own included

getParameter() throws ParameterNotFoundException for a name that was never set — it does not return null. Ask hasParameter() first, or catch it.

A custom parameter never changes the digits. Only the secret, the digest, the digits and the counter or the period and the epoch do that.

docs.title: The image parameter
docs.text:
The one custom parameter with an established meaning. FreeOTP and a few others load it as the icon of the account:

$totp = $totp->withParameter('image', 'https://example.com/logo.png');

otpauth://totp/alice%40example.com?image=https%3A%2F%2Fexample.com%2Flogo.png&secret=JBSWY3DPEHPK3PXP

It is not part of the key URI format, and no list of the applications that honour it is maintained. An application that does not read it ignores it, so the cost of setting it is nothing.

docs.title: What not to put there
docs.text: Everything in a provisioning URI reaches the user's device and lives in whatever backup that device makes. It is also, in most applications, exportable as plain text. Store identifiers if you must, nothing confidential, and nothing you rely on coming back unchanged: the URI is held by the user, not by you.

docs.title: The counter
docs.text:
A parameter of HOTP only. It is the number that replaces the clock: both sides must agree on how many codes have been consumed.

use OTPHP\HOTP;

$hotp = HOTP::generate()->withCounter(1000);
echo $hotp->getCounter(); // 1000

The default is 0, which is where RFC 4226 starts and what to use for a new account. Any value from 0 up is accepted; a negative one throws InvalidParameterException.

It travels in the provisioning URI, so the user's device starts from the same place:

otpauth://hotp/alice%40example.com?counter=1000&secret=JBSWY3DPEHPK3PXP

docs.title: It moves on its own
docs.text:
This is the one piece of state the library keeps. On a successful verify(), the counter is set to one past the value that matched:

$hotp = HOTP::createFromSecret($secret)->withCounter(1000);

$hotp->verify($codeFor1000);  // true
$hotp->getCounter();          // 1001

It is why HOTP is the only class in the library not marked @readonly, and it is deliberate: the code that was just accepted can never be accepted again by the same object. Every code below the new counter is burned with it.

at() does not move it. Only verify() does, and only on success.

docs.title: Persist it, or the protection is gone
docs.text:
The object is thrown away at the end of the request. If you do not write the counter back, the next request starts from the old value and accepts the same code again — which is exactly the replay the increment exists to prevent.

use OTPHP\HOTP;

$hotp = HOTP::createFromSecret($user->getOtpSecret())
    ->withCounter($user->getOtpCounter());

if (! $hotp->verify($code, null, 5)) {
    return false;
}

$user->setOtpCounter($hotp->getCounter());  // not optional
$entityManager->flush();

return true;

Store the provisioning URI instead of the secret and the same rule applies: write the URI back after every successful verification, because the counter it carries has changed. See What to store.

docs.title: Going out of step, and catching up
docs.text:
Each code the device produces advances its counter, whether or not the code reaches you. A button pressed by accident leaves the device ahead of the server, and its next code will not match the counter you hold.

The window is the repair: it tests the counters above yours and, on a match, jumps to just past it.

$hotp->verify($code, null, 10);  // tests counter … counter + 10

Five to ten covers accidental presses. See The window.

Verifying against an explicit counter lower than the object's returns false immediately, without testing anything: counters only move forward.

docs.title: The digest and the digits
docs.text: Two parameters shape the code itself: the hash the HMAC uses, and how many of the resulting digits are kept. Both must match on the server and in the user's application, exactly.

docs.title: The digest
docs.text:
The default is sha1. That is not an oversight: in HMAC, SHA-1 has no known weakness that matters here, and it is what every authenticator application supports.

$totp = $totp->withDigest('sha256');
echo $totp->getDigest();

Use sha1, sha256 or sha512. They are the three values RFC 6238 defines, the three the otpauth:// key URI format names, and in practice the only three an authenticator application will read. SHA-2 is preferable where you control both ends.

The value is accepted if hash_hmac_algos() lists it and its output is at least 19 bytes. Anything else throws InvalidParameterException:

$totp->withDigest('md5');      // 16 bytes: rejected
$totp->withDigest('crc32');    // not an HMAC algorithm: rejected
$totp->withDigest('sha3-256'); // accepted by the library; no application will read it

Why short digests are refused, since v11.5

The RFC 4226 truncation reads four bytes starting at an offset taken from the low four bits of the last digest byte — an offset anywhere from 0 to 15 — so it reads up to the 19th byte. With a 16-byte hash such as MD5, that read runs past the end of the digest, and the generated code collapses onto a small set of values that barely depend on the secret. It is a real weakness in the verification path, not a theoretical one.

Before v11.5 the library accepted md5 and produced those codes. An account provisioned that way was never interoperable and was never safe: re-enrol it with a supported algorithm. Upgrading turns the silent weakness into an exception, which is the point. See From v11 to v12.

docs.title: The digits
docs.text:
The default is 6, which is what users expect and what every application displays.

$totp = $totp->withDigits(8);

The accepted range is 1 to 10. Outside it, InvalidParameterException:

$totp->withDigits(0);  // "Digits must be between 1 and 10."
$totp->withDigits(11); // same

Ten is not an arbitrary limit. The truncation yields a 31-bit number, at most 2 147 483 647, so the eleventh digit would carry no entropy at all — and 10 ** $digits would overflow PHP's integer range on the way. The library refuses rather than produce a code that only looks longer.

Codes are zero-padded on the left, so six digits always render as six characters:

echo $totp->at(1_519_401_289); // "626112" — and "042…" would keep its leading zero

Going above 6 is safe as long as the user's application follows; Google Authenticator ignores the parameter and keeps showing six. See Authenticator applications.

docs.title: Changing them later
docs.text: Both appear in the provisioning URI, so a change affects only the accounts enrolled after it. Every earlier account keeps the parameters it was provisioned with, and will stop authenticating if you switch the server to new ones without re-enrolling. This is the single best reason to store the whole provisioning URI rather than the secret alone: see What to store.

docs.title: The label and the issuer
docs.text:
These two name the account inside the user's authenticator application. They have no effect on the digits — they exist for the provisioning URI, where they become the line the user reads in their list of accounts.

What it holds Example Label The account alice@example.com Issuer The service My Service 
use OTPHP\TOTP;

$totp = TOTP::createFromSecret('JBSWY3DPEHPK3PXP', $clock)
    ->withLabel('alice@example.com')
    ->withIssuer('My Service');

Set the issuer. A user with accounts on four services, all labelled with the same e-mail address, cannot tell the four entries apart without it.

docs.title: Neither may contain a colon
docs.text:
The otpauth:// format uses a colon to separate the issuer from the account inside the path, so a colon in either value would be ambiguous. Both : and its encoded forms %3A and %3a are refused, with InvalidLabelException.

Do not build the issuer:account form yourself

A label such as My Service:alice@example.com passes withLabel() — it looks like the issuer ":" accountname grammar, which is valid in a URI the library reads. But building the URI rejects it, so the failure surfaces later, at getProvisioningUri():

$totp = $totp->withLabel('My Service:alice@example.com'); // accepted
$totp->getProvisioningUri();                              // InvalidLabelException

Put the account in the label, the service in the issuer, and let the library join them.

docs.title: What the URI looks like
docs.text:
With both set, the issuer appears twice: as the prefix of the path, and as a query parameter. That duplication is what the key URI format asks for, and applications differ in which one they read.

echo $totp->getProvisioningUri();

otpauth://totp/My%20Service%3Aalice%40example.com?issuer=My%20Service&secret=JBSWY3DPEHPK3PXP

To keep the prefix and drop the query parameter:

$totp = $totp->withIssuerIncludedAsParameter(false);
echo $totp->getProvisioningUri();

otpauth://totp/My%20Service%3Aalice%40example.com?secret=JBSWY3DPEHPK3PXP

There is rarely a reason to. Keep both unless an application you must support chokes on the parameter.

docs.title: At least one of them is required
docs.text:
Building a provisioning URI with neither throws InvalidLabelException: The label is not set. Either label or issuer must be set. An object with only an issuer produces a URI whose path is that issuer, which is legal but tells the user nothing about which account it is.

Nothing requires a label for verification. An object built only to check a code can leave both unset.

docs.title: Reading them back
docs.text:
The factory undoes the join: the prefix of the path is removed from the label and becomes the issuer.

$otp = Factory::loadFromProvisioningUri(
    'otpauth://totp/My%20Service%3Aalice%40example.com?issuer=My%20Service&secret=JBSWY3DPEHPK3PXP',
    $clock
);

$otp->getLabel();   // "alice@example.com"
$otp->getIssuer();  // "My Service"

When the prefix and the parameter disagree — which Microsoft Office 365 does, among others — the parameter wins. See The factory.

docs.title: The parameters
docs.text:
An OTP object is a bag of named parameters. The password it produces is a function of all of them, so two objects that differ in any one produce different codes — and a user whose application holds the first cannot authenticate against the second.

Parameter Applies to Default Page secret both 64 random bytes The secret algorithm both sha1 The digest and the digits digits both 6 The digest and the digits period TOTP 30 seconds The period and the epoch epoch TOTP 0 The period and the epoch counter HOTP 0 The counter label both none The label and the issuer issuer both none The label and the issuer anything else both — Custom parameters

The first group changes the digits. The label and the issuer do not: they name the account in the authenticator application and appear only in the provisioning URI. Setting them on a verification-only object is pointless, and leaving them unset makes getProvisioningUri() throw.

docs.title: Reading them
docs.text:
$totp->getSecret();
$totp->getDigest();
$totp->getDigits();
$totp->getPeriod();        // TOTP
$totp->getEpoch();         // TOTP
$hotp->getCounter();       // HOTP
$totp->getLabel();         // null if unset
$totp->getIssuer();        // null if unset

$totp->getParameters();            // all of them, as an array
$totp->hasParameter('image');
$totp->getParameter('image');      // ParameterNotFoundException if absent

docs.title: Writing them
docs.text:
Every parameter has a with*() method. Each returns a new object, leaving the one you called it on untouched, so they chain and the original stays usable:

use OTPHP\TOTP;

$base = TOTP::generate($clock);

$configured = $base
    ->withDigest('sha256')
    ->withDigits(8)
    ->withLabel('alice@example.com');

$base->getDigits();        // 6 — unchanged
$configured->getDigits();  // 8

Forgetting the assignment is the one mistake this style invites:

$totp->withDigits(8);         // does nothing you can observe
$totp = $totp->withDigits(8); // this is what you meant

The full list: withSecret(), withDigest(), withDigits(), withLabel(), withIssuer(), withIssuerIncludedAsParameter(), withParameter(), plus withPeriod() and withEpoch() on a TOTP and withCounter() on a HOTP.

docs.title: The deprecated setters
docs.text:
Each with*() has a set*() twin that mutates the object in place and returns nothing. They are deprecated since v11.4 and removed in v12.0, when the classes become readonly:

// Deprecated
$totp->setDigits(8);

// What to write
$totp = $totp->withDigits(8);

Finding them in a project:

grep -rn -- '->set[A-Z]' --include='*.php' src/

From v11 to v12 has the full mapping and the patterns worth knowing.

docs.title: They are validated when they are set
docs.text:
A parameter is checked by its own validator the moment you set it, not when the code is generated. An invalid value throws immediately — InvalidParameterException for most of them, InvalidLabelException for the label and the issuer:

$totp->withDigits(0);          // InvalidParameterException: Digits must be between 1 and 10.
$totp->withDigest('md5');      // InvalidParameterException: too short for the truncation
$totp->withLabel('a:b:c');     // InvalidLabelException

See Exceptions.

docs.title: The period and the epoch
docs.text:
Two parameters exist on a TOTP only. They decide where one code ends and the next begins.

timecode = floor((timestamp - epoch) / period)

docs.title: The period
docs.text:
How long a code lives, in seconds. The default is 30.

$totp = $totp->withPeriod(60);
echo $totp->getPeriod();   // 60
echo $totp->expiresIn();   // seconds before the current code changes

It must be at least 1; otherwise InvalidParameterException.

Thirty seconds is what to use. Google Authenticator ignores any other value and keeps counting in thirties, so a different period silently breaks it. A longer period is also a longer window of opportunity for a stolen code, and a shorter one leaves users retyping codes that expired while they were reading them.

The period bounds the window too: a window must be strictly smaller than it.

A code does not live for a full period from the moment you show it. It lives until the end of its period, which may be one second away — that is what expiresIn() is for.

docs.title: The epoch
docs.text:
Where the counting starts, as a Unix timestamp. The default is 0, the Unix epoch, which is the T0 of RFC 6238. Leave it there unless you have the specific need below.

$totp = $totp->withEpoch(1_519_401_289);
echo $totp->getEpoch();

It must be 0 or more. A timestamp earlier than the epoch has no timecode, and asking for one throws InvalidParameterException.

Shifting the epoch shifts every period boundary. Set it to the exact moment a code was produced and that moment becomes the start of a period, so the code is valid for the whole period that follows rather than for whatever remained of a boundary-aligned one:

use OTPHP\TOTP;

$totp = TOTP::createFromSecret($secret, $clock)->withPeriod(5);

$password = $totp->at(1_519_401_289);  // the period holding that second ends at 1519401289
$totp->verify($password, 1_519_401_289); // true
$totp->verify($password, 1_519_401_290); // false — a new period began

$aligned = $totp->withEpoch(1_519_401_289);

$password = $aligned->at(1_519_401_289);  // this period runs from 1519401289 to 1519401293
$aligned->verify($password, 1_519_401_289); // true
$aligned->verify($password, 1_519_401_293); // true
$aligned->verify($password, 1_519_401_294); // false

That is useful for a code you send yourself — by e-mail or by text message — where you know when it was created and want it to live for a known duration. Both sides must agree on the epoch, so it travels in the provisioning URI like the rest.

A fixed epoch with a fixed secret repeats itself

If you store the creation timestamp as the epoch and keep the same secret, the first code of the first period is the same every time: same secret, same timecode 0, same digits. Use a fresh secret for each code you generate this way — deriving it from the timestamp is one way — or you will be sending the same password over and over.

Google Authenticator does not read the epoch parameter. Only use it where you control both ends.

docs.title: The secret
docs.text: The shared secret is the credential. It is held as an upper-case Base32 string, which is the encoding authenticator applications read and the one the provisioning URI carries.

docs.title: A generated one
docs.text:
generate() draws it from random_bytes(). The default is 64 bytes — 512 bits, 103 Base32 characters:

use OTPHP\TOTP;

$totp = TOTP::generate($clock);
echo strlen($totp->getSecret()); // 103

A second argument sets the size in bytes:

$totp = TOTP::generate($clock, 20); // 32 characters
$hotp = HOTP::generate(20);         // HOTP takes the size as its first argument
Bytes Base32 characters 16 26 The minimum worth using 20 32 What RFC 4226 recommends, and what most services issue 32 52 64 103 The default

A size below 1 throws InvalidParameterException.

Why 20 bytes is often the better choice

The strength of the construction is capped by the hash it uses — 160 bits for sha1, 256 for sha256 — so a secret longer than that adds nothing an attacker has to work through. What it does add is a much denser QR code, which some cameras and some applications read badly. Twenty bytes is the size RFC 4226 recommends, and 32 is a reasonable choice next to sha256.

docs.title: Your own
docs.text:
use OTPHP\TOTP;
use ParagonIE\ConstantTime\Base32;

$secret = Base32::encodeUpper(random_bytes(20));
$totp = TOTP::createFromSecret($secret, $clock);

The value is normalised on the way in: it is upper-cased, and trailing = padding is stripped. So the secret you read back may not be character-for-character the string you passed, while decoding to the same bytes.

Whatever produces it must be a cryptographically secure source. random_bytes() is one; rand(), uniqid(), a hash of the user's e-mail address and a timestamp are not.

docs.title: When it is decoded
docs.text:
The Base32 string is decoded lazily, the first time a code is computed. A secret that is not valid Base32 is therefore accepted by createFromSecret() and only fails later, at now(), at() or verify(), with a SecretDecodingException:

use OTPHP\TOTP;
use OTPHP\Exception\SecretDecodingException;

$totp = TOTP::createFromSecret('INVALID!@#$%', $clock); // accepted

try {
    $totp->now();                                       // throws here
} catch (SecretDecodingException $e) {
    // "Unable to decode the secret. Is it correctly base32 encoded?"
}

If you validate a secret a user pasted by hand, call now() on it and catch that exception; constructing the object proves nothing.

docs.title: Storing it
docs.text: One secret per account, never shared, never reused for a second purpose. It is a credential that grants valid codes forever to whoever reads it, so encrypt it at rest with a key kept outside the database, and keep it out of logs and error reports. See Security recommendations and What to store.

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text:
Requests for new features, bug fixes and all other ideas that make the library more useful are welcome. Issues go to the bug tracker; a security issue goes to security@spomky-labs.com instead, and never to the tracker.

The conventions a pull request is expected to follow are in CONTRIBUTING.md.

docs.title: Which branch
docs.text: Branches are named <major>.<minor>.x. Open a pull request against the lowest maintained branch your change applies to: a bug fix against the oldest branch that has the bug, a new feature against the branch under development. Changes are then merged forward into the newer branches.

docs.title: The checks
docs.text:
Quality tasks run through Castor, from castor.php at the root of the library. Each one runs in a dockerized image, or natively when Docker is not available.

castor phpunit      # the test suite, with coverage
castor phpstan      # static analysis, at the maximum level
castor ecs          # coding standards
castor rector       # modernisation, as a dry run
castor deptrac      # the dependency rules between layers
castor prepare-pr   # the fixers, then the analysers: what to run before pushing

A single test, by name:

castor phpunit -- --filter TOTPTest::testGenerateOTPAt

Continuous integration runs the suite on PHP 8.2, 8.3 and 8.4, on 8.5 experimentally, and once more on 8.2 with the lowest allowed dependencies.

docs.text:
The pages of this site live in Spomky-Labs/otphp-doc, one branch per version of the library. Every page has an edit pencil at the top that opens it on the right branch.

make install   # the toolchain, in .venv

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
composer require spomky-labs/otphp

That is all. The library has no service to register, no configuration file and no bundle.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• PHP 8.1 or later. The only extension the library calls into is hash, which is bundled with PHP and cannot be turned off.
  • A PSR-20 clock, for TOTP. See below.

Three dependencies come with the package, all small:

Package What it is for paragonie/constant_time_encoding Base32, encoded and decoded without a timing side channel psr/clock The ClockInterface a TOTP reads the time from symfony/deprecation-contracts The function that emits the deprecation notices

docs.title: A clock, for TOTP
docs.text:
A time-based password needs to know what time it is, and the library does not decide that for you: you pass a PSR-20 clock. It becomes mandatory in v12.0, so pass it now.

composer require symfony/clock

use OTPHP\TOTP;
use Symfony\Component\Clock\NativeClock;

$totp = TOTP::generate(new NativeClock());

Any PSR-20 implementation will do; lcobucci/clock is another. In your own services, inject the clock rather than building one where you need it — that is what makes a test able to decide what time it is. See The clock.

HOTP counts uses, not seconds, and needs no clock.

docs.title: Checking it works
docs.text:
use OTPHP\TOTP;

$totp = TOTP::createFromSecret('JBSWY3DPEHPK3PXP', new NativeClock());

echo $totp->now();          // six digits
echo $totp->expiresIn();    // the seconds left before they change

JBSWY3DPEHPK3PXP is the secret of every example in these pages and in the RFC test vectors. It is public. Never give it to a real account.
