docs.title: Security recommendations
docs.text: OTPHP decides whether a code matches a secret. Whether that answer protects an account depends on the things around it, and those are yours to build. This page is the list of them.

docs.title: Treat the secret as a credential
docs.text:
A one-time password secret is not a password hash. It is a shared secret: whoever reads it can produce valid codes forever, silently, from anywhere. A leaked OTP table is a leaked second factor for every account in it.

  • Encrypt it at rest, with a key held outside the database.
  • Never log it, and never put it in an error message, a stack trace or a bug report. The provisioning URI contains it in full.
  • Never send it to a third party. That includes the online QR code generators; see QR codes.
  • Generate one per account, from the library. TOTP::generate() uses random_bytes(); nothing else is acceptable as a source.

docs.title: Rate-limit verification
docs.text:
Six digits are one million values, and a TOTP accepts a whole period's worth of guesses. Without a limit, an attacker who holds the password walks through the second factor in hours.

Count failures per account, not per IP address, and lock the factor after a handful. A lockout that the user can lift by signing in again is enough; a silent counter that never trips is not.

docs.title: Refuse a code twice
docs.text:
The library has no memory. A TOTP it accepted at second 1 of a period it will accept again at second 29, which is long enough for a code read over someone's shoulder, or captured by a phishing page, to be replayed.

Store the last accepted timecode — or the last accepted code — with the account, and refuse anything that is not newer.

For HOTP the library does keep the counter moving: verify() increments it on success, so the same code cannot be used twice against the same object. That only holds if you persist the counter after every successful verification. See The counter.

docs.title: Keep the window small
docs.text:
The window exists because clocks drift, not because users are slow. Every second of window is another code an attacker may guess with.

A window of a few seconds covers a phone whose clock is slightly off. A window close to the period roughly triples the codes you accept. See The window.

docs.title: Choose the parameters once, and record them
docs.text:
Use sha1, sha256 or sha512; they are the only digests the specifications define and the only ones authenticator applications read. SHA-2 is preferable. Digests shorter than 19 bytes are rejected outright — the RFC 4226 truncation cannot work with them — and that rejection is a real defence, not a formality. See The digest and the digits.

Six digits and a thirty-second period are what every application expects. Eight digits are fine if your users' application supports them, and nothing else is worth the interoperability it costs.

Whatever you choose, store it alongside the secret, or store the whole provisioning URI. A parameter you change later invalidates every account provisioned with the old one. See What to store.

docs.title: Confirm enrolment
docs.text:
Ask the user for one valid code before you turn the factor on. A QR code that was scanned by nothing, or by an application whose clock is wrong, otherwise locks the account at the next sign-in.

Issue recovery codes at the same time, and treat them like passwords: hashed, single-use, countable.

docs.title: Serve the enrolment page over HTTPS, and only to the owner
docs.text: The QR code is the secret, rendered. Show it once, to an authenticated session, over TLS, and do not let it be fetched again afterwards. Caches, proxies and browser history are all places it should not land.

docs.title: Reporting a vulnerability
docs.text: Security issues in OTPHP go to security@spomky-labs.com, never to the public issue tracker. The process, and the versions that receive fixes, are in SECURITY.md.

docs.title: What OTPHP is
docs.text:
A one-time password is a short number derived from a secret shared between your server and the user's device, and from something that changes: the time, or a counter. Both sides compute the same number from the same inputs, so the user proves they hold the secret without sending it.

OTPHP is the PHP implementation of that computation, in both of its standard forms.

Specification Algorithm What changes RFC 4226 HOTP A counter, incremented at each use RFC 6238 TOTP The time, in slices of a fixed period

The provisioning URI, the otpauth:// address a QR code carries, follows the Key Uri Format Google Authenticator defined and the other applications adopted.

docs.title: The public surface
docs.text:
It is small on purpose. Four classes you will name, with an interface each, in the OTPHP namespace — plus the exceptions of OTPHP\Exception, and InternalClock and Url, which are marked @internal and are not yours to use.

Class What it is TOTP A time-based password. Holds a PSR-20 clock HOTP A counter-based password Factory Reads an otpauth:// URI back into a TOTP or a HOTP OTP The shared, abstract parent. Holds the parameters and the RFC 4226 truncation

TOTPInterface and HOTPInterface both extend OTPInterface; Factory implements FactoryInterface. Type your own services against the interfaces: they are what the library promises not to break inside a major version.

docs.title: Which inputs matter
docs.text: An OTP object is a bag of parameters, and the password it produces depends on all of them. Two objects with the same secret and different digests produce different codes, and a user whose application was configured with one cannot authenticate against the other. The parameters are listed in The parameters; the consequence is in What to store.

docs.title: What it leaves to you
docs.text:
OTPHP verifies a code against a secret. Everything that makes that verification mean something lives in your application:

  • Storage. The secret is a credential. Where it goes and how it is protected is your decision.
  • Replay. A TOTP stays valid for its whole period. Nothing here remembers that a code was already accepted thirty seconds ago.
  • Rate limiting. Six digits are a million possibilities, which is not many. Unlimited attempts defeat the factor entirely.
  • Enrolment and recovery. Showing a QR code, confirming the first code, issuing recovery codes, letting a user remove the factor.

Security recommendations covers each of these.

docs.title: The release process
docs.text:
Releases are versioned as <major>.<minor>.<patch>, following Semantic Versioning. A version may carry a suffix such as -rc1 for an early access build; those are pre-releases.

What changed What comes out A backwards-compatible bug fix A patch version Functionality added, backwards-compatibly A minor version An incompatible API change A major version

docs.title: Backwards compatibility
docs.text:
You can upgrade from one minor version to the next with confidence. When a feature, an enhancement or a fix cannot keep backwards compatibility, it waits for the next major version.

Two exceptions:

  • Experimental features and code marked @internal are outside this policy. OTPHP\InternalClock is one of them.
  • A backwards compatibility break is tolerated when a security issue requires it. The 19-byte minimum on digests, which landed in v11.5, is such a case.

docs.title: Maintained versions
docs.text:
Release branches are maintained for the three most recent minor releases; fixes, security fixes included, may be backported to them depending on severity and feasibility. The current list is in RELEASES.md, and the security policy in SECURITY.md.

Older versions are not maintained. A pull request against one may be considered, without any guarantee.
